events.event: First Black newspaper founded — Freedom's Journal founded in New York City — the first African American newspaper; the start of the archiveable Black press.
Philadelphia Tribune founded — Christopher James Perry Sr. founds the Philadelphia Tribune; it becomes the oldest continuously published African-American newspaper in the US.

Baltimore Afro-American begins — The Home Protector becomes the Afro-American; in 1897 John H. Murphy Sr. buys the press with $200 borrowed from his wife Martha, founding the Murphy family ownership line.
New York Amsterdam News founded — James Henry Anderson founds the Amsterdam News in San Juan Hill, Harlem, with $10 and a hand-written six-page first edition; one of ~50 Black-owned papers in the US.
Pittsburgh Courier founded — The Pittsburgh Courier is founded; under Robert L. Vann it becomes the most influential Black paper of the mid-20th century.
First issue of The Crisis — The NAACP's official magazine debuts with W. E. B. Du Bois as founding editor; it will become a central venue of the Harlem Renaissance.
Associated Negro Press founded — Claude Barnett founds the ANP in Chicago - the first national news service for African-American newspapers, twice-weekly packets to ~150 US and ~100 African papers.

Opportunity: A Journal of Negro Life begins — The National Urban League launches Opportunity under editor Charles S. Johnson; its 1924-27 literary contests will discover Hughes, Hurston, Cullen and others.
Sadie Warren buys the Amsterdam News — Anderson sells the Amsterdam News to Sadie Warren; it will be resold to physicians Powell and Savory around 1935-36.
Schomburg collection joins NYPL — Arturo Schomburg's personal collection is added to NYPL's 135th Street Branch, winning the collection international acclaim.
St. Louis American founded — First issue appears; founded by Judge Nathan B. Young Jr. and Black businessmen including Homer G. Phillips as an eight-page paid tabloid (~2,000 circulation).
Atlanta Daily World founded (weekly) — William Alexander Scott II, 26, founds the Atlanta World as a weekly; it becomes a daily in 1931-32 - the first successful African-American daily.

Jack L. Cooper's 'The All-Negro Hour' premieres on Chicago's WSBC, the first radio program with an all-Black cast (precedence for absolute 'first' is disputed by 1927-1928 series documented by OTRR researcher Ryan Ellett).
Houston Defender founded — Clifton F. Richardson Sr. (earlier founder of the Houston Informer, 1919) founds the Houston Defender weekly.
Los Angeles Sentinel founded — Leon H. Washington Jr. publishes the first issue of the Sentinel (begun as the Eastside Shopper); it becomes the largest paid Black-owned weekly in the West.
William Alexander Scott II assassinated — Scott is shot and killed outside his home at age 32; the murder is never solved.
Garland begins at Pittsburgh Courier; ANP peaks — Hazel B. Garland joins the Courier as a freelancer; the ANP serves ~225 subscribers at its peak mid-1930s strength.
Michigan Chronicle founded — John H. Sengstacke founds the Detroit paper with Louis E. Martin as first editor; Martin arrives June 6, 1936 with a $5 raise and a one-way bus ticket.
NNPA founded — Sengstacke organizes Black publishers to found the National Negro Publishers Association (renamed NNPA in 1956) to harmonize "Negro journalism."
NNPA founded in Chicago — Twenty publishers led by John H. Sengstacke meet in Chicago and found the National Negro Publishers Association (renamed NNPA in 1956).
Double V campaign launched — The Pittsburgh Courier launches the Double V campaign - victory against fascism abroad and racism at home - adopted across the Black press.
Johnson Publishing Company founded — John H. Johnson founds the Johnson Publishing Company, seeding the largest Black print empire of the 20th century.

First Black reporter at a presidential press conference — Atlanta Daily World reporter Harry McAlpin becomes the first Black reporter to cover a presidential press conference (Roosevelt, then Truman).
Ebony debuts — John H. Johnson's Ebony publishes its first issue with a 25,000-copy press run that sells out; named by his wife Eunice Walker Johnson.
Ebony's first issue — First issue of Ebony, dated November 1, 1945, reaches 25,000 readers.

Ebony first Black magazine audited by ABC; Courier peaks — Ebony becomes the first Black magazine tracked by the Audit Bureau of Circulations (309,715); the Pittsburgh Courier's circulation peaks (~357,000-400,000).
LOC microfilms 150+ Black newspapers — The Library of Congress and the ACLS microfilm 150+ African American newspapers (12 reels) — the first large-scale preservation of the Black press.
WDIA Memphis signs on as a white-owned station airing country, light pop, and block programming.
Nat D. Williams launches 'Tan Town Jubilee' on WDIA, among the first US radio programs designed for a Black audience; the first publicly recognized Black DJ in the segregated South.
Opportunity ceases — Opportunity publishes quarterly from 1942 and ceases in 1949 after 26 years as the Urban League's journal.
Jesse B. Blayton Sr. buys WERD Atlanta for $50,000, making it the first radio station both owned and programmed by African Americans; 'Jockey Jack' Gibson becomes its star DJ.
Andrew 'Skip' Carter founds KPRS in Kansas City (founding year variously reported as 1949, 1950, or 1952); it becomes the oldest continuously Black-owned radio station in America.
Jet founded — JPC launches Jet, the weekly digest of Black news.
Jet founded — John H. Johnson launches Jet as "The Weekly Negro News Magazine," a digest-size Black newsweekly.
Robert C. Meeker buys KCOH Houston, establishing the first Black-owned station in Texas with all-Negro programming on the Gulf Coast.
The National Negro Network, founded by W. Leonard Evans Jr., launches as the first Black-owned radio network (up to 45 affiliates); it collapses within a year for lack of capital.
WDIA is licensed for 50,000 watts and moves to 1070 kHz; its signal reportedly reached ~10% of the US African-American population.
Jet publishes Emmett Till open-casket photos — At Mamie Till Bradley's request, Jet publishes photos of her son's open casket - a landmark act of civil-rights photojournalism.
sources: NPR via KSUT; The Oklahoma Eagle

events.event: NNPA renamed; Chicago Defender goes daily — The National Negro Publishers Association is renamed the National Newspaper Publishers Association; Sengstacke converts the Chicago Defender from weekly to daily.
Houston Forward Times founded — Julius P. Carter founds the Houston Forward Times to unite Black Houston; his wife Lenora "Doll" Carter and daughter Karen Carter Richards will continue it.

Muhammad Speaks first edition — The Nation of Islam newspaper Muhammad Speaks publishes its first edition under Elijah Muhammad; it will reach ~850,000-950,000 circulation per edition in the early 1970s.
sources: Final Call history; Black Archives of Mid-America

events.event: ANP ceases (disputed); Washington Informer founded — The Associated Negro Press is listed as defunct in 1964 (one source says it continued until Barnett's 1967 death); Calvin W. Rolark founds the Washington Informer with $500.
sources: Wikipedia; African American Registry; DC Preservation

events.event: Muhammad Speaks goes weekly — Muhammad Speaks moves from monthly to weekly on February 12, 1965.

Sengstacke buys the Pittsburgh Courier (year disputed) — Sengstacke purchases the declining Pittsburgh Courier (reported as 1965 or 1966); it ceases Oct 22, 1966 and is relaunched as the New Pittsburgh Courier in 1967.
Pittsburgh Courier financial collapse — The Pittsburgh Courier collapses financially under owner John H. Sengstacke.
Pittsburgh Courier ceases; relaunched 1967 — The Pittsburgh Courier ceases publication; Sengstacke buys and relaunches it as the New Pittsburgh Courier in 1967.
Blayton retires and sells WERD (call sign becomes WXAP in 1972).
WGBH Boston launches Say Brother, three months after MLK's assassination — a weekly public-affairs program produced by, for, and about the Black community.
Under executive producer William Greaves, Black Journal launches; it wins an Emmy in 1969.
Black Journal premieres on NET as a monthly public-affairs series 'for blacks, about blacks'; first episode includes Coretta Scott King speaking at Harvard.
Byron Lewis founds UniWorld Group, the longest-standing Black-owned multicultural ad agency.
Percy Sutton and Black shareholders found Inner City Broadcasting Corporation in New York; its first purchase is WLIB (AM).
Inner City Broadcasting Corporation founded by Percy Sutton, Clarence Jones and 50+ Black shareholders — anchor of Black-owned radio.
Essence and Black Enterprise debut — Essence's first issue appears (April/May 1970; initial circulation ~50,000); Black Enterprise's first issue (August 1970) features Charles Evers on the cover.
Black Enterprise founded by Earl G. Graves Sr.; hit newsstands August 1970.
Earl G. Graves Sr. launches Black Enterprise magazine.
Sutton/Jones group buys the Amsterdam News — Percy E. Sutton and Clarence B. Jones lead an all-Black group purchasing the Amsterdam News from Dr. Clilan B. Powell.
WBLS hits New York airwaves as the only Black-owned FM station in the city's history; the WBLS acquisition year is also reported as 1972/1974.
Tony Brown takes over leadership of Black Journal as executive producer and frequent host.
Tom Burrell founds Burrell Communications Group in Chicago.
The Mutual Broadcasting System founds the Mutual Black Network, the first national full-service news network aimed at African Americans (98 affiliates).
Ronald and Judith Davenport found Sheridan Broadcasting Corporation in Pittsburgh with four stations.
Inner City Broadcasting acquires WLIB, its first station, programmed to New York's Black community.
Black Press Archives founded at Howard — The Black Press Archives is founded as a joint Howard University/NNPA project at the Moorland-Spingarn Research Center.
The National Black Network launches in New York with 25 affiliates, the first coast-to-coast Black-owned radio network.

Hazel B. Garland named editor of New Pittsburgh Courier — Sengstacke appoints Garland editor-in-chief - the first African-American woman to edit a national newspaper; the paper wins the 1976 Russwurm Award.
NOI transition; Muhammad Speaks renamed — After Elijah Muhammad's death, W. D. Muhammad takes over the Nation and the newspaper is renamed (Bilalian News, later The Muslim Journal).
NABOB (National Association of Black Owned Broadcasters) is organized in Atlanta, the first trade association for Black broadcast owners.
Melvin Lindsey brings 'The Quiet Storm' to WHUR-FM's late-night lineup at Howard University; the format spreads to nearly every urban station's night slot.
Sheridan Broadcasting buys 49% of the Mutual Black Network.
Black Journal leaves public TV for commercial television with Pepsi sponsorship, renamed Tony Brown's Journal.
Black Classic Press founded — W. Paul Coates founds Black Classic Press in Baltimore to republish out-of-print works by and about people of African descent.
The FCC creates the Minority Tax Certificate Program, incentivizing station sales to minorities; it drives the main wave of Black broadcast ownership.
The Final Call founded — Louis Farrakhan launches The Final Call in the basement of his home as the Nation of Islam's official newspaper.
Sheridan Broadcasting buys the rest of the Mutual Black Network and renames it the Sheridan Broadcasting Network.
Cathy Hughes buys WOL-AM Washington, D.C. for ~$995,000 after 33 loan rejections, founding Radio One with an urban talk format.
Robert L. Johnson launches BET, a cable channel for Black audiences.
BET launched; Radio One founded — BET hits the air as the first Black-owned cable network; Cathy Hughes buys WOL-AM, founding Radio One.
BET launches as a two-hour weekly block on the Madison Square Garden Sports Network, founded by Robert L. Johnson ($15K loan + $500K from John Malone); logo designed by Cheryl D. Miller.
Suggs buys the St. Louis American — Donald Suggs and investors buy majority shares (Suggs majority stockholder/publisher in 1984) and convert the paper from paid limited circulation to a free weekly.
WLIB becomes the second station in the nation with a Black news-talk format (after WOL).
Tony Brown's Journal returns to public television (PBS).
BET becomes a full-time standalone cable channel (some sources say 1983).
Thomas family buys the LA Sentinel — Kenneth R. Thomas and Jennifer Thomas purchase the Los Angeles Sentinel from the Washington estate.
Tom Joyner begins his eight-year 'Fly Jock' double-shift: mornings at KKDA-FM Dallas, afternoons at WGCI-FM Chicago.
BET News launches with Ed Gordon anchoring the first half-hour news program directed at a Black audience.
Ruth Washington dies — Ruth Washington - who led the Sentinel after her husband's 1974 death - dies; the Thomas era continues under Jennifer Thomas from 1997.
The Sheridan Broadcasting Network merges with the National Black Network to form American Urban Radio Networks (some sources date the completed merger to 1995).
BET becomes the first Black-controlled company on the New York Stock Exchange.
BET becomes the first Black-owned company listed on the NYSE.
BET IPO — BET's IPO makes it the first Black-controlled company listed on the NYSE.
Byron Allen founds Entertainment Studios (later Allen Media Group).
Byron Allen founds Allen Media Group (as Entertainment Studios).
sources: Allen Media Group press materials via PR Newswire

events.event: The Tom Joyner Morning Show premieres in national syndication on ABC Radio Networks; it peaks at 120+ markets and 15+ million daily listeners.

Essence Music Festival launches; BCP Digital Printing founded — Essence launches the Essence Music Festival for its 25th anniversary; W. Paul Coates launches BCP Digital Printing, which will account for ~85% of BCP revenue.
Congress repeals the Minority Tax Certificate Program; minority broadcast ownership begins a long decline.
Minority Tax Certificate repealed — Congress repeals the Minority Tax Certificate, removing the key incentive for selling broadcast stations to minority owners.
Telecommunications Act of 1996 — The Telecommunications Act abolishes broadcast ownership limits, triggering consolidation that decimates Black station ownership.
The Telecommunications Act of 1996 is signed, lifting radio ownership caps and triggering consolidation: Clear Channel grows from ~86 to ~1,200 stations; Black-owned station counts fall.
Sengstacke dies; chain enters family trust — John H. Sengstacke dies; his four-paper chain is held in a family trust.
Say Brother becomes Basic Black (producer Cynthia Johnson: title more inclusive of women).
Radio One goes public (6.5M shares at $24), making Cathy Hughes the first African American woman to chair a publicly held company.
Publicis takes a 49% stake in Burrell Communications — one of a wave of mainstream-agency alliances with Black agencies.
Time Inc. buys 49% of Essence; NNPA Media Services launches — Time Inc. purchases 49% of Essence Communications; the NNPA launches Media Services for print/web ad placement.
Viacom acquires BET, ending its run as a Black-owned company (deal value disputed: $2.3B vs ~$3B).
WPP acquires a 49% stake in UniWorld Group; Byron Lewis calls it 'a matter of survival' against mainstream agencies chasing Black-consumer budgets.
Viacom agrees to buy BET Holdings Inc. for $2.3B in stock plus $570M in assumed debt (figures vary $2.3B-$3B across sources); announced late 2000.
sources: USA Today via readabstracts; Wikipedia: BET Media Group

events.event: Walter P. Lomax Jr. purchases WURD 900 AM Philadelphia (year also reported as 2003), creating Pennsylvania's only Black-owned talk station.
Viacom-BET deal closes; BET networks join MTV Networks. BET is no longer Black-owned.
BET sold to Viacom (~$3B) — Viacom acquires BET Holdings for ~$3 billion, ending Black ownership of the network; Robert L. Johnson becomes the first Black billionaire.
Real Times buys the Sengstacke chain — Detroit-based Real Times buys the four-paper chain (New Pittsburgh Courier, Michigan Chronicle, Atlanta Daily World, Tri-State Defender) for nearly $12 million.
Tom Joyner co-founds Reach Media to gain ownership of his syndicated show.
Sengstacke chain sold to Real Times — The Sengstacke newspaper chain is sold to Real Times for ~$12M, consolidating remaining Black papers.
Radio One and Comcast announce a joint venture to create a TV network for African Americans 25-54.
TV One launched — Urban One launches TV One in partnership with Comcast, extending the Radio One survival model into cable.
TV One launches on MLK Day with Comcast carriage in Atlanta, Detroit, Washington, Baltimore; Johnathan Rodgers president/CEO.
Bakewell buys the LA Sentinel — Danny Bakewell purchases the Los Angeles Sentinel from Jennifer Thomas, becoming executive publisher/chairman/CEO.
Radio One acquires 53% of Reach Media for $56.1 million, taking over syndication of the Tom Joyner Morning Show.
Time Inc. completes Essence takeover; Johnson dies — Time Inc. buys the remaining 51% of Essence, ending Black ownership; John H. Johnson dies August 8, 2005.
John H. Johnson dies; JPC begins its terminal decline.
Robert Johnson retires; Debra L. Lee becomes BET CEO (some sources say 2006).
Steve Harvey launches The Steve Harvey Morning Show on Premiere Radio Networks (iHeart), becoming Joyner's direct competitor on non-Black-owned syndication.
Rev. Delman Coates leads 'Enough is Enough' protests — 500 protesters at Debra Lee's DC home — over BET's stereotypical content; campaign meets with BET leadership.
Mellon grant: AFRO archives project — A Mellon Foundation grant funds Johns Hopkins/Morgan State students to inventory the AFRO archives at the newspaper's headquarters.
The Boondocks airs episode satirizing BET executives Lee and Reginald Hudlin over reality-TV programming.
Tony Brown's Journal ends on PBS after 26 years there (40 years total lineage).
The Root founded by Henry Louis Gates Jr. and Donald E. Graham as a digital Black newspaper.
The Root launches, co-founded by Henry Louis Gates Jr. and Donald E. Graham under the Washington Post Company (Slate Group).
TV One president Johnathan Rodgers announces extensive Democratic National Convention coverage.
Sirius and XM merge into SiriusXM, consolidating Black-formatted satellite channels (Heart & Soul, The Heat, etc.) under one corporate owner.
TheGrio launches as a division of NBC News, founded by the team behind the documentary 'Meeting David Wilson.'
OWN: Oprah Winfrey Network launches, replacing Discovery Health, as a 50/50 Discovery/Harpo joint venture.
Comcast solicits 100+ proposals for minority-owned independent networks under NBCUniversal merger commitments.
Bounce TV announced as the first 24/7 over-the-air Black broadcast network; founders include MLK III and Andrew Young.
Creditors force Inner City Broadcasting's subsidiary into Chapter 11 bankruptcy on $254 million in debt.
Bounce TV launches at noon ET as a digital-subchannel broadcast network.
Bounce TV launched — Bounce TV launches as the first 24/7 digital multicast network targeting African Americans.
Atlanta Black Star founded by Neil 'Jelani' Nelson, Tracy Dornelly, and Andre Moore (Diamond Diaspora Media).
Byron Lewis retires and sells his remaining UniWorld stake to Monique Nelson and family; firm later rebrands as UWG (2014).
Comcast announces distribution deals for four minority-owned networks, including Aspire (Magic Johnson/GMC) and Revolt (Sean Combs).
Aspire TV launches (some sources say June 30, 2012) targeting positive images of African Americans.
Viacom pulls 26 channels including BET from DirecTV (~20M homes) in carriage-fee fight; blackout lasts until July 20.
YMF Media LLC (Ron Burkle + Magic Johnson) buys 15 Inner City stations for $180 million, then breaks up the group in 2013-2014 sales.
KCOH sells its 1430 Houston signal to the La Promesa Foundation for $2.14 million, ending 59 years as a Black-owned station.
REVOLT Media & TV founded by Sean 'Diddy' Combs (with Andy Schuon).
Revolt launches in New York City, Los Angeles, and Chicago.
Roberts Broadcasting sells its last three full-power stations to Ion Media; zero Black-owned and operated full-power TV stations remain in the US.
Blavity founded by Morgan DeBaun, Aaron Samuels, Jonathan Jackson, and Jeff Nelson, targeting Black millennials.
Jet ends print publication, going digital-only, as print advertising collapses.
Angelica Nwandu founds The Shade Room as an Instagram-based media company.
Jet ends print — Jet ends regular print publication (720,000 circulation) and converts to a digital magazine app in July 2014; JPC sells Ebony/Jet to Clear View Group in 2016.
Urban One acquires Comcast's stake in TV One, taking full control.
Byron Allen files $20B racial-discrimination suit against Comcast under Section 1981 over refusal to carry his channels.
Byron Allen sues Comcast ($20B) and Charter ($10B) under Section 1981 of the Civil Rights Act of 1866 over refusal to carry his channels.
Univision Communications acquires The Root from Graham Holdings (price undisclosed; ~5M monthly uniques per comScore).
Sherrell Dorsey founds The Plug, a daily tech newsletter covering Black founders and the innovation economy.
JPC sells Ebony/Jet to Clear View — JPC sells Ebony and Jet to Clear View Group; the magazines' final corporate chapter under Johnson ownership ends.
BET acquires Soul Train library — BET acquires the Soul Train brand and library (1,100+ episodes, 40 specials) from InterMedia/Yucaipa.

Access.1 Communications takes 100% ownership of AURN, forcing out Sheridan's 51%; Sheridan later goes out of business. AURN's effective Black ownership becomes contested (Access.1 reported controlled by Guggenheim Capital Partners).
Johnson Publishing sells Ebony and Jet to Clear View Group, a Black-owned private equity firm.
Byron Allen's Entertainment Studios (Allen Media Group) acquires TheGrio.
Allen acquires TheGrio — Byron Allen's Entertainment Studios acquires TheGrio, keeping it 100% Black-owned.
Blavity closes a $1M seed round led by 500 Startups (followed by ~$1.8M in additional seed funding).
Radio One is renamed Urban One; WURD expands to 96.1 FM.
Discovery increases its OWN stake from 50% to 73%.
Blavity launches 21Ninety and acquires Shadow and Act and Travel Noire.
Scripps acquires Bounce TV (Katz) — E.W. Scripps acquires the Katz networks including Bounce TV, taking Black-targeted OTA TV into general-market ownership.
E.W. Scripps announces purchase of Bounce (and Katz Broadcasting) for $292M; deal closes Oct 2, 2017.
Allen Media Group acquires The Weather Channel.
Essence returns to Black ownership — Richelieu Dennis's Essence Ventures LLC acquires Essence from Time Inc., restoring fully Black-owned status.
Scott Mills becomes BET president as Debra Lee cedes day-to-day duties; Lee steps down May 28, 2018 after 32 years.
Facebook rolls out the 'meaningful interactions' News Feed algorithm shift; Chartbeat measures publisher referral declines; LittleThings shuts down in February after ~70% Facebook traffic loss.
Essence Ventures acquires Essence Communications from Time Inc.; Essence returns to 100% Black ownership.
Essence returns to Black ownership — Essence Ventures acquires Essence from Time Inc., returning the brand to 100% Black ownership.
Essence Ventures (Richelieu Dennis) acquires Essence Communications from Time Inc.; brand returns to 100% Black ownership with equity for the all-Black female executive team.
Byron Allen acquires The Weather Channel (~$300M) from NBCUniversal/Bain Capital.
Blavity raises $6.5M Series A led by GV (Comcast Ventures, Plexo Capital, Baron Davis Enterprises participate).
BET+ streaming service launches with Tyler Perry as a minority investor (reported 25%).
G/O Media formed by Great Hill Partners from Univision's Gizmodo Media Group + The Onion; The Root folded into the portfolio.
Cleo TV, TV One's sister network for millennial/Gen Z Black women, launches.
Great Hill Partners buys Gizmodo Media Group from Univision; The Root becomes part of the newly created G/O Media.
JPC files Chapter 7 bankruptcy — Johnson Publishing Company files for Chapter 7 bankruptcy; its archive goes to auction.
Karen Carter Richards elected NNPA chair — The Houston Forward Times publisher is elected national chair of the NNPA, succeeding Dorothy Leavell.
Foundation consortium buys JPC archive ($30M) — A four-foundation consortium buys the JPC archive for $30M, rescuing 3-4 million images and A/V from the bankruptcy.
ANA/AIMM's U.S. Multicultural Media Forecast (PQ Media) published: multicultural ~40% of population but only 5.2% of ad/marketing spend; African-American media $7.2B.
The final live Tom Joyner Morning Show airs, ending a 25-year syndication run; affiliates move to the Rickey Smiley Morning Show.
59 digitized Black Journal episodes (1968-1977) released to stream free via the American Archive of Public Broadcasting.
Charlamagne Tha God launches the Black Effect Podcast Network as a joint venture with iHeartMedia.
Supreme Court rules 9-0 against Allen in Comcast case (but-for causation standard); parties settle in June 2020 with Comcast carrying Comedy.TV, Recipe.TV, JusticeCentral.TV.
Supreme Court rules unanimously in Comcast v. NAAOM that Section 1981 plaintiffs must prove race was the but-for cause of the refusal to contract.
Earl G. Graves Sr., founder of Black Enterprise, dies at 85; son Earl 'Butch' Graves Jr. continues leading the company.
On Juneteenth, BET launches $25M 'Content for Change' social-justice initiative (adopted company-wide by ViacomCBS).
Allen settles with Comcast: carriage of Comedy.TV, Recipe.TV, JusticeCentral.TV on Xfinity plus amended Weather Channel terms.
BOMESI launched — BOMESI launches around Juneteenth as a network of 300+ Black-owned publishers to confront the <2% ad-spend inequity.
NABOB states Black people own fewer than 180 of 11,000+ US commercial radio stations (~1.6%), 52 years after the Kerner Commission.
Ebony forced into bankruptcy by creditors amid unpaid debts and freelancer lawsuits.
Essence furloughs staff amid COVID-19 losses, paying salaries through the week and benefits through the furlough.
Bridgeman buys Ebony for $14 million — After bankruptcy, Ebony is purchased by Bridgeman Sports and Media and relaunches March 1, 2021 as a digital-first brand, "Moving Black Forward."
Discovery increases OWN ownership from 73% to 95%; Harpo remains minority stakeholder.
Junior Bridgeman's Bridgeman Sports and Media wins Ebony's assets out of bankruptcy for $14M; brand goes digital-first.
Bridgeman buys Ebony/Jet ($14M) — Bridgeman Sports and Media buys Ebony and Jet out of bankruptcy for $14M.
Allen Media Group acquires HBCU GO (launched 2012) and BET Studios launches under BET CEO Scott Mills with equity for Black creators.
iONE Digital (Urban One) acquires Bossip, MadameNoire, and HipHopWired from Moguldom Media Group.
TheGrio.TV launches (rebranded from MGM's Light TV) on MLK weekend with Fox O&Os as launch group, reaching 100M+ households.
Allen settles the $10B racial-discrimination suit against Charter Communications.
Ebony digital relaunch — Ebony relaunches as a digital publication under Bridgeman ownership.
15 of 16 full-time The Root staffers resign amid conflict with G/O Media leadership; EIC Danielle Belton departs for HuffPost.
Apple rolls out App Tracking Transparency (iOS 14.5), curtailing cross-app ad tracking — a flagged but unverified risk for ad-dependent Black publishers.
Group Black launches (Dennis, Bough, Montaque) with a $75M GroupM commitment toward a stated $500M goal for Black-owned media.
Word In Black founded (soft-launched May 2021): ten Black newspapers launch a shared national digital platform via the Fund for Black Journalism.
Word In Black founded — Ten legacy Black newspapers launch Word In Black, incubated by the Local Media Foundation.
MRC suspends Nielsen's national and local TV ratings accreditation after pandemic-era undercounting; VAB had petitioned citing undercounting of Black, Hispanic and young viewers.
Roland Martin launches the Black Star Network, a free, ad-supported, Black-owned OTT network.
VAB publishes research asserting 30 billion ad impressions went uncounted by Nielsen, including 7 billion Black and 5.5 billion Hispanic impressions (seller-side advocacy study).
Capital B launches as a nonprofit news organization (national + Capital B Atlanta), co-founded by Lauren Williams and Akoto Ofori-Atta.
Capital B launched — Capital B launches as a nonprofit, donor-funded news organization for Black audiences.

Black Press Archives digitization funded; LOC adds titles — Howard's MSRC receives a $2M Jonathan Logan Family Foundation grant to digitize the Black Press Archives; LOC adds 1,224 pages from 103 Black titles to Chronicling America.
Knight Foundation announces $4M+ three-year investment in publishers of color, including Capital B and URL Media.
NABOB and BIA Advisory Services release the first authoritative 'Black Owned Radio Stations Ownership & Revenue Report.'
JPC archive transferred to NMAAHC/Getty — The JPC archive's ownership is formally transferred to the NMAAHC and the Getty Research Institute; Getty commits $30M to digitization.
Blavity launches Home & Texture and restructures into Blavity Media Group + DEI Solutions Group after doubling 2022 ad revenue.
Paramount Global explores selling majority stake in BET Media Group; bidders include Tyler Perry, Byron Allen, Diddy, Group Black, 50 Cent, Kenya Barris.
MRC restores accreditation of Nielsen's national TV ratings after 19-month suspension; local ratings remain unaccredited.
Paramount backs off talks to sell majority stake in BET after interest from Tyler Perry, Byron Allen and Group Black; Perry later calls the process 'disrespectful.'
Paramount ends BET sale process — Paramount ends its process to sell BET Media Group; BET stays in corporate hands despite bids from Black owners.
Paramount cancels BET sale ('wouldn't result in any meaningful deleveraging'); Perry calls process 'disrespectful.'
Google's Helpful Content Update rolls out; independent publishers report steep search-traffic losses (self-reported 40–90%).
Burrell Communications acquired by FVLCRUM Funds-led consortium; Tara DeVeaux named CEO; MBE designation maintained.
Sean Combs steps down as REVOLT chairman amid sexual-assault lawsuits.
Sean Combs takes leave from Revolt amid sexual-assault lawsuits; sells stake March 2024.

Coates receives Literarian Award; AFRO at 132 years — W. Paul Coates receives the National Book Foundation's 2024 Literarian Award; the Baltimore AFRO marks 132 years under Murphy-family leadership (Dr. Frances "Toni" Draper).
860 AM Atlanta (the original WERD frequency, as WAEC) goes dark after 76 years when Beasley Media sells the tower site.
AIMM reports diverse-owned media drew 2.5% ($1.9B) of the largest media holding companies' spend in 2023, up from 2.2% in 2022 — far below population-representative levels.
Word In Black converts from a Local Media Foundation-incubated project to an independent public benefit corporation.
Word In Black becomes a public benefit corporation — the first national Black-news collaboration with that structure.
Meta announces deprecation of the Facebook News tab in the US and Australia (effective April 2024); no new commercial news deals.
REVOLT announces employees are now its largest shareholder group after Combs' shares are fully redeemed and retired.
Revolt announces employee-majority ownership (Combs shares redeemed/retired), keeping the company Black-owned under CEO Detavio Samuels.
Skydance/Paramount $8.4B merger approved; reported $1.6-1.7B sale talks for BET with BET CEO Scott Mills' investor group; BET suspends Hip Hop Awards and Soul Train Music Awards indefinitely.
Wilmington Journal building demolished — The Wilmington Journal building (a Black press building) is demolished in North Carolina — a documented physical loss of Black media heritage.
Nielsen's Big Data + Panel national TV measurement receives MRC accreditation; endorsed as upfront currency for 2025.
Burrell acquires Atlanta agency Fitzco, launching BCG Worldwide as a Black-owned agency network.
TheGrio carries out sweeping layoffs (managing editor, podcast/video teams) as part of Allen Media Group-wide cuts.
Essence Communications sues Group Black over alleged unpaid bills ($7M); Group Black countersues in June, claiming a debt-to-equity deal.
New Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison confirms BET is NOT for sale and will anchor the company's streaming strategy; Black-led acquisition bids (Perry, Allen, Mills-led group) end.
BET publishes 'When Google AI Summarizes, Black Websites Pay the Price,' warning AI Overviews threaten Black-owned sites (The Grio, Blavity, Okayplayer, AfroTech).
Ashley Allison's Watering Hole Media acquires The Root — G/O Media's last remaining outlet — returning it to Black ownership.
Ashley Allison's Watering Hole Media acquires The Root from G/O Media, returning it to Black ownership.
iHeartMedia extends Charlamagne Tha God's deal (reported $200M, five years), continuing the Black Effect Podcast Network joint venture (60+ shows, 11M monthly downloads claimed).
Two legacy Black papers close (Portland Skanner, Richmond); Onyx Impact commits $500,000 to Black-owned media including NNPA.
FCC approves DuJuan McCoy's Circle City Broadcasting acquisition of Indianapolis ABC affiliate from Scripps ($83M) — rare expansion of Black broadcast ownership.
Allen Media Group renews long-term portfolio carriage with YouTube TV (Weather Channel, Comedy.TV, Recipe.TV, JusticeCentral, Local Now); Allen's family office takes majority stake in BuzzFeed, Inc.
Urban One Q1 2026: revenue decline but narrowed net loss ($3.1M), $60.2M debt reduction, and portfolio moves — acquiring KKDA/KRNB (Dallas) for $22M from Black-owned Service Broadcasting.
Amistad lays off half its staff — The Amistad Research Center lays off half its staff after federal funding cuts, showing the fragility of Black archival infrastructure itself.
Essence Ventures acquires Beautycon Media, consolidating another Black-founded beauty/festival brand under Richelieu Dennis's holding company.
